I played this game for a few hours, and my actual computer was in the game! It took away a lot of the fear I had of messing something up, and I was able to take apart my computer, and clean/fix everything and put it back together. I wouldn't have done that if it wasn't for this game really showing me how easy it actually is.
Super unrealistic. I was able to order a high end GPU and have it delivered next day at a reasonable price.
This game is one of the greatest works of fantasy of all time. It takes place in a realm and era in which GPUs existed

My wife and I owned and operated a custom PC shop for 15 years. Our builds were all customized according to what customers intended to do with them. So I came into this game with a lot of knowledge and expectations. My own system(s) are connected to HDTVs. They're my entertainment centers with all TV, movies, guitar recording, games - everything I do at home goes through my computer(s). 

So let's start with what this game does well. It's very good at showing basic parts and where they go, the screws and how components are placed is pretty accurate. Someone wanting to learn the basics could learn a lot from the game. It's a very stable game. Has crashed on me a few times when first starting the game and the first few steps around the shop - otherwise has not crashed on me. My outdated GTX 950, i5 4690, and 24GB of RAM (not a typo) runs it very well at highest settings, although a bit mind boggling that I can hear my GPU fan scream at times I wouldn't expect it - like checking emails. Overclocking is fairly accurate although there are only major changes for CPU clock and bus speeds. It's been a while since I overclocked many components in real life but I remember having much finer adjustments than the game provides. However if you're patient, you can underclock the multiplier pretty drastically and overclock the base to get finer increments - just remember to adjust your RAM accordingly.

What it doesn't do very well is provide additional PC parts such as USB hubs, TV Tuners, additional PCI cards and such. It also allows RAM to be placed in any slot instead of in correct channels, although it does seem to benefit from more than 1 RAM stick. I've never built a system in real life or in the game without at least 2 sticks of RAM for the dual channel benefit.  And in real life, you can mix RAM sticks to some extent, you're just bound by the lesser timings. The game doesn't show timings at all and doesn't allow mixing sticks - not even the same brand and speed with different sizes. In real life, you have access to every PC part from day 1. I understand the game had to find ways to progress as you go along, but it drives me crazy that I can't access a powerful PSU to use GTX 980s in SLI when they become available. It's not until many levels later that PSUs stop being the main constraint, and more so than customer budgets. I understand it was probably done for support by companies, but I can count on 1 hand the number of times a customer asked for a PC to play a certain game at certain settings, and I've never been asked to benchmark my PCs. Not once. We stress tested them, which is completely different. I assume this was done to get 3D Mark to allow their name to be used. And 3D Mark is extremely GPU dependent - fine for gamers but the rest of the world benefits more from better CPUs and more RAM. Too bad the game doesn't include Sisoft Sandra or other benchmarking tools for programs other than games and Adobe Photoshop.

What it does terribly is fix known issues. (EG: the Cooler Master Masterbox won't allow the PCI lock to be attached with a GPU installed, nor with the correct PCI slots installed once they've been removed). Crazy! Water cooling is severely limited, 1 reservoir (until you reach level 30), so 1 loop. And only 1 way to install reservoirs makes it very unrealistic. And way too often a radiator in one area prevents another in the same area even when they're miles apart (such as top or front only allowing 1 x 120mm radiator when there's actually room for 2 or 3). And water cooling is often less efficient than air - in real life that's rarely true. The game temps are better from many radiators instead of bigger ones (EG: 2 separate 120mm radiators cools much better than a single 3x120mm radiator). That's just wrong.

My biggest complaint comes from parts binning and when they become available. It's true that no 2 components will perform identically. But I've never seen 2 high end GPUs perform 10-13 degress C differently - they wouldn't pass QA inspection with that poor performance. The cheaper the GPU in real life, the more likely you are to get a bad one. But high end components must meet much stricter requirements - the game seems completely opposite.

So would I recommend this game? Must admit that once I reached level 30 and achieved 26,000 3D Marks, I was sad to see that there was nothing more to do in the game. So yes, I obviously enjoyed it and would recommend it to anyone who is interested in building and fixing PCs. It's far from a perfect simulation but it also does many things very well. I found it a very enjoyable experience overall. :)

A marketing tool cleverly masked behind an addictive zen-ish PC building simulator.

You spend each day fulfilling orders coming in, ranging from cleaning dusts and viruses to building PC of sufficient specs to run specific softwares (which are real-life softwares... imagine the sponsored marketing dollars) within certain budgets and deadline. And gosh, I hate it when customers requested that I use cables of specific colours.

It's almost educational enough to give you a GENERAL understanding on pc parts compatibility and how overclocking works. In real life, there are more considerations that are missing/insufficiently represented in the game. Eg. Lower tolerances on overclocking settings to fry your components, different chassis and MOBO combination affecting gfx card choices and layouts due to form factors and layout, differentiating SATA/IDE/M.2 slots, fan size/speed/location affecting airflow and efficiency of cooling effects, etc.

Was trying to build a non-gaming work PC in real life recently and I found myself inadvertently biased to choose parts intended for a monster gaming rig.

Summary: Addictive, Zen, Educational, Subliminal Marketing. You are warned.

If you strive for a perfect 5 star review from your customers, re read the entire email before finishing. Make sure to do everything they want or hint towards. If you have trouble with the 3D Mark jobs I built a small formula I use in a notepad for each 3D Mark job I have running to keep track and properly calculate.

For eg. (VC is Video Card)
"Customer Name" - "PC's score" 3DMark, Current VC  "VideoCard Score", Increase by "", upgrade with "New Part"

M.Mercury - 3379 3DMark, Current VC 2560, Increase by 174, upgrade with "MSI Radeon R9 390X"


When I get a 3DMark job I duplicate the above formula and start filling it in. I click on "PC Stats" in the email to get the PC's current 3DMark Score (Didn't notice this at first and always ran my own taking much longer)

so with this example 

M.Mercury wants a new 3DMark of 3553

M.Mercury - 3379 3DMark, Current VC 2560, Increase by 174, upgrade with "MSI Radeon R9 390X"


3379 was accomplished with his current VC that has a 2560 3DMark rating
The new 3DMark "3553" Minus the current 3DMark "3379" (3553 - 3379 = 174)
I need to upgrade either my CPU or Video Card by 174 to reach 3553
Current VC 2560 + 174 = 2734.  

Buy the "Part Ranking" software from the store to find the current Video Card 3DMark Rank
Our final number is 2734. Buy any Video Card with a ranking of 2734 or higher that you found from the Part Ranking software and then add the item you purchased at the end of the formula. I do this because if I do several jobs (which I often do) there is a risk I might use a video card that was meant for a 3DMark job which will cause them to fail. Using this formula I can easily do 4+ 3DMark type jobs with out worry. I'm also able to figure out exactly what to buy the same day I accepted the job so the PC arrives along with its upgrade. No need to run 3DMark Software on the PC to figure out what i'd need to buy.
This may not be perfectly accurate and I could be missing some stuff but so far its working great for me. 

I'm excited to continue and discover more things PCBS can offer.
I hope this review can be of help to some people :D

This game is so much more fun than I thought it would be. The devs thought of everything! It's exactly what it sounds like-- you run a shop; people bring you PC's to fix. Sometimes they tell you exactly what they want ("please upgrade my graphics card"), and sometimes they don't ("I don't know what needs upgraded, but I want a 3D-Mark score of 3500"). You even have to use popular apps like 3D Mark, or for instance, use a version of "Can I Run It" when a customer wants to hit minimum or recommended specs in a certain game... very cool! 

You diagnose PC's; you order parts (including choosing the shipping speed depending on how much you want to spend vs how quickly you want it); you deal with customers who leave you reviews depending on how you do; you collect payment; you upgrade your shop; you manage your money (you even have to pay the shop's rent and utility bills); you can even try to save money by installing used parts in people's PC's (as in: parts you took out of other customer's PC's when upgrading them)-- but watch out, not all customers are cool with used parts!

I really appreciate that the devs clearly went the extra mile. For example, I'm lazy and like to play games with an Xbox One controller sitting on my couch. But what are the chances that they would integrate perfect Xbox One controller support into an obviously KB&M-centric game like this? Well, they did! I couldn't believe it. I literally installed a *MAJOR* AAA 1st person title from Ubisoft just last night, and I couldn't even play it with an Xbox One controller without doing a bunch of outside config. But PC Building Simulator has native controller support? That should tell you all you need to know about whoever made this game. I get the impression it was probably a smaller team, and IMO, they earned my money.

PC Building Simulator 1 offers a unique and immersive experience for both seasoned PC builders and newcomers to the world of computer hardware. Developed by The Irregular Corporation, this simulation game provides an authentic and detailed simulation of assembling and maintaining a custom PC.

Graphics and Interface:
The game boasts crisp, detailed graphics that make each component and tool easily distinguishable. The interface is intuitive, with well-designed menus and tooltips that guide players through the building process seamlessly.

Gameplay:
PC Building Simulator excels in its gameplay mechanics. Players start with a modest workshop and gradually expand their business by completing orders from virtual customers. The process of selecting components, installing them in the case, and troubleshooting any issues feels remarkably true-to-life. The simulator also includes a variety of real-world components from popular manufacturers, allowing players to experiment with different configurations and designs.

Learning Experience:
One of the most commendable aspects of PC Building Simulator is its educational value. For those unfamiliar with PC hardware, the game serves as an excellent introduction, teaching players about the function and compatibility of various components. With the included tutorial and extensive in-game resources, players can learn valuable skills that translate to real-world PC building.

Customization and Expansion:
The game offers extensive customization options, allowing players to personalize their workshop with decorations and equipment upgrades. Additionally, regular updates and DLCs introduce new components and features, ensuring that the experience remains fresh and engaging over time.

Community and Modding Support:
PC Building Simulator benefits from an active community of players and modders who contribute to the game's longevity. From user-created components to workshop designs, the modding scene adds a wealth of content and creativity to the game, further enhancing its replayability.

Final Thoughts:
Overall, PC Building Simulator is a superbly crafted simulation game that caters to both enthusiasts and newcomers alike. Its attention to detail, educational value, and engaging gameplay make it a must-have title for anyone interested in PC hardware or simulation games. Whether you're looking to hone your PC building skills or simply enjoy a relaxing virtual workshop experience, PC Building Simulator delivers on all fronts.

PC Building Simulator was on its way to become one of the top simulator games. But instead of a final touch that would make everything come together, the devs decided to dumb it down and ruin their previous work with nonsensical decisions that instantly sent their game to the biggest category on steam, a "Could have been". Yes, PCBS could've been great, but it's not.

- Possibly the best example of this are the "Diagnose & Fix" jobs, where your virtual customers ask you to, you know, diagnose and fix whatever is wrong with their machine. Not only they literally tell you whats wrong (I guess its my mobo!), you are given a budget worth exactly the broken part, to a dollar. This turns these jobs into a puzzle grind, where you just check the sum and buy the part, there is zero investigation involved. But even if you deliberately ignore these hints, there is no variety: Does the pc start? If it does, its the gpu or hdd. If not, its the mobo or psu. Just mindless clicking.

- The rating system is an abomination that only highlights how little freedom you have in this game. Did you replace customers Mtech with an Mtech plus? Oh god, rating goes down. Did you exceed the budget by 15$? Rating down. You didnt change cables for colored ones for free? Rating. Down. It really feels like a puzzle where you're not allowed to do anything else than what the game specifically tells you to. It doesn't feel like a game, it feels like a job, a chore. Even if you're a good boy and get your rating to 5 stars, the only reward is more of the same jobs that have a 100$ more for labor.

- 3DMark. Installing OS takes 5 seconds and so does virus scanning. So why in the fuck does 3dmark take a MINUTE and a HALF? It cant be that bad, youre thinking, but no. Every other job requires you to run it (even hdd replacement jobs) and it also happens to be the only way to boost the value of your pc's you sell on pcbay. No matter how you plan your work, no matter how fast or slow you are at multitasking, you WILL have to wait for the same animation to finish over and over.
A good game shouldnt make you alt tab every two minutes. It feels like cheap filler to stretch the gameplay.

- There are many beatiful cases, some of them which have exclusive art. But what does that matter if in 95% of jobs the budget forces me to buy the cheapest one for 40$? I'm sure this had to take quite a lot of effort, so why is this part ignored is beyond me. At least some kind of visual rating + jobs that work with it would've been nice.

- Optimization is still very poor and the end-of-the-day bug, present for months, is still there.

All in all, it's a shame. It's obvious lots and lots of love was put into PCBS initially, the core of the game is great, writing (of story emails) is absolutely awesome, but all of these huge gameplay flaws simply make it a No, not recommended.

I bought this game knowing nothing about computers. Like, I thought RAM was just something that made my PC go fast. But now? I can actually recognize parts, build a system, and even troubleshoot stuff (in-game... baby steps 😅).

PC Building Simulator makes learning feel easy and fun. The tutorials are clear, the tasks ease you in, and Free Build mode lets you mess around without pressure. Plus, everything uses real brands—so if you're thinking of building a PC in real life, this is actually a great place to start.

It’s chill, it’s satisfying, and I never thought I'd enjoy plugging in virtual power cables this much. 10/10 would accidentally forget thermal paste again.

As someone who's done this exact thing for nearly 9 years for a living, I recommend it. It's definitely not a replacement for hands-on experience, it's far too simplified and the only people who could learn something from it are (in my opinion) those who have never seen the inside of a real PC. But it's kinda relaxing and just... nice.

The music is repetitive, the 3DMark lottery is infuriating at times, the game doesn't punish you for constantly reusing scavenged parts (no warranty mechanic, probably a plus) and the tasks are often very unrealistic, but fit the simplicity of the game. 

I'd say the tasks being super repetitive is kind of a part of the simulation, the real thing is like that too. What's definitely not like the real thing - in my experience - are all those fancy cases, cooling, cards etc., but again, doing a hundred HP/Dell/Whatever office prebuilts in a row would probably put people off! I could also probably count the number of customers who even knew about benchmark scores on my fingers. Hell, if most people asked me to beat certain scores all the time I might have quit a lot sooner than I did.

I love this game. I wanted to learn how to build a custom computer from basic components. A friend recommended this game and I'm really glad they did. While the game is far simpler than building a computer in real life, it does a great job of teaching what the fundamental parts are, how they fit together, and the basic approach to finding compatible combinations. It even goes into (very over-simplified) methods of tuning and over-clocking your CPU, RAM, and GPU.  And it does it all in a surprisingly fun way, and with components that actually have real-life counterparts.

Fair warning: Any computer you assemble in the game is not guaranteed to work as well (or have the same compatibility) as the real-world analog, so this does not stand in for a part picker. But it was quite amusing to be able to assemble my real-world rig inside the game with the same corresponding parts.

Even once you pass all the story jobs, the game is still enjoyable, as the equipment keeps evolving. The developers regularly add new components as they come to market in the real world, so you can keep building bigger and better desktop rocket ships.

Tips for new players:
* You'll definitely want to invest in any and all screwdriver upgrades as soon as possible. That part of the game gets a little tedious pretty quickly.

* Be prepared for occasional frustration, when a time-constrained job comes in that requires parts you haven't unlocked yet (that only happened to me in the early game).

* Twice I made the mistake of accepting a customer repair/upgrade job on the same day it was due. Since the customer's rig doesn't show up until the next morning, it was an automatic failure. Seems like a bug, tbh, but easily avoidable if you're paying attention.

This game teaches the basics and is quite spot on when it comes to building a PC. It would be nice to see some standardized builds, meaning you put the motherboard together before you install the assembly into the case. It would be nice to have this functionality with it being a simulator. Ram slot configuration is not up to par as you can install them in any slot you want and they are somehow seemingly recognized by the BIOS. Overclocking is by no means close to what real world scenarios prove, as I would never be able to increase voltage in components that the game allows vs real world attempts for stability. As an IT professional in-game, I would also like to see some more advanced projects added on a software side vs only the hardware side. Add things that real life IT personnel have to deal with, and it doesn't have to be complicated. I spent an entire day working with an IT guy over the phone once trying to solve an issue with a motherboard and a NVMe M.2. It happens. But it doesn't have to be that complicated lol. Server side PC's, dual CPU setups, Xeon CPU's. Why not add Quadro Cards for clients looking to do some decent workstation loads? I do believe the Dev's can go a lot further in actually making this better as a simulator, which in turn, will allow a more immersive gameplay to the people that enjoy the game.

Honestly, this is the first simulator game I picked up out of curiosity given that it's something i'm interested in. 

For what it's worth it does (at the very least) teach you the rudementary basics, but doesn't go into advanced techniques, and definitely doesn't really go into/account for other nifty tricks that you can do whilst building computers, but it's hell of enjoyable, and the free-build mode at least gives you a little bit of visual splendor. It's definitely a fun game to pass time with and get more familiar/comfortable around the process that goes into building computers.

If I had one major complaint, it's how automated a lot of the processes are. A complete newbie isn't going to know that Item A goes into slot A, etc etc, so having them have to manually plug it in versus it doing it for you would kind of help give them a better sense of direction, and instill a more realistic knowledge into them.

Maybe make it an option in the future that cable management is something they have to do, because as it stands some of these PC's can look really janky, and that's just not visually pleasing or efficient in the least.

While not directly stated, I appreciate how the game is willing to go into details about part compatibility from time to time. One of the biggest threats to new PC enthusiast is buying a bunch of parts and not realizing that they're incompatible with eachother. I'm glad the game takes a bit of time to address this issue, and it does teach them a small bit regarding compatibility.

The Overclocking in this game is a bit wierd, not used to what i'm working with but it does (at least) get the job done for the purpose of explaining what it does, and what sort-of-kinda it's used for. I lament the poor bastard who turns their clock rates up too damned high and winds up BSOD'ing their PC due to them taking this game's systems at face value.  They should talk about some of the negative consequences of overclock, because this game instills the idea that overclocking = free performance boosts at no real consequence other than possibly BSOD'ing because you put in the wrong values. 

Another minor complaint in the music-choice. It gets grating after awhile, so muting the music and putting on some chillhop made it 1,000x more bearable. 

It gets a solid 7.5/10, and I would recommend it to people who are brand-new to give them a general idea while maybe taking some time to explain the finer-points with a real-life example. No two PC's are 100% alike, afterall.

You play as the owner of a PC repair shop. You perform tasks such as building a PC from scratch, upgrading a PC, replacing broken PC parts, changing the colour of cables inside a PC, running a virus scan, and cleaning dust from a PC. Satisfy your customers to earn money, improve your shop's rating, and level up.

+ Relative Accurate Simulation
+ Humorous E-mails

- Grindy
- Unrealistic Customers
- No PCPartPicker Equivalent
- Budget Doesn't Matter

The only strength of PC Building Simulator is that it's a relative accurate simulation. Various potential PC problems are accounted for in the simulation, although the way they manifest may not be fully accurate. However, there isn't much praise to give in terms of actual game play. Despite the fact that most of your customers aren't experienced enough to upgrade a computer themselves, they are somehow experienced enough to accurately diagnose the exact component that is broken in their computer. They seem to automatically know if you gave them used parts rather than new parts, or if you tried to downgrade their PC. This leads to most repair jobs simply being a matter of buying the parts that they said was broken, and maybe changing their cables, doing a virus scan, or cleaning out dust on top of it. What's even stranger is that you will sometimes receive requests to upgrade a customer's PC not to run a specific app or play a specific game, but to hit a specific number on a benchmark. Nevertheless, most of the time these customers have a large enough budget that you can simply upgrade to the best PC parts available, rather than try to squeeze out the most performance with the least amount of money spent. Finally, while you do have to be more budget conscious when building a new PC from scratch, the lack of a PCPartPicker equivalent makes this task rather tedious as your only tool is a notepad and mental math.

Conclusion: Maybe it's fun if you've never built a PC before and want to see how everything is put together, but there is no satisfaction to correctly troubleshooting problems, picking out PC parts, staying within budget, or doing a clean build. Doesn't scratch the PC Building itch for me.

PC Building Simulator is like that time you watched a YouTube video of someone assembling a computer and thought, "I could totally do that." Then you tried, and your computer exploded metaphorically, of course. But with this game, it’s more like a safe, virtual explosion where your dignity remains intact, and you only need to reset the software every 45 seconds.

Let’s talk game play: The premise is simple you’re running a PC repair shop and your job is to build, upgrade, and troubleshoot computers. Think of it as House Flipper, but with a lot more dust and wires that seem to have a vendetta against you. You’ll start by installing a graphics card the wrong way, probably fry a few components, and then realise you’ve just spent 30 minutes trying to figure out why the power button isn’t working (pro tip: it's not plugged in).

The “Realistic” mode is an absolute thrill, where you get to deal with customer orders that are just vague enough to make you question your life choices. Is it really the power supply that’s busted, or are they just saying that because they’re secretly running Bitcoin mining software and don't want you to know? The suspense! The drama!

And let’s not forget about the impeccable customer service. There's nothing more satisfying than receiving an order for a computer that “just needs a little tweaking,” only to realise you’ve been sent on a wild goose chase to install a 10TB hard drive and “optimise the airflow,” all while trying to figure out how the heck to clean a case without accidentally damaging everything in sight. Pro tip: Just vacuum everything with your laptop running, it’s fine.

But honestly, the highlight is the actual building process. You get to play around with different components, click on things, and watch as they either magically fit together like a perfect Lego set or fail miserably like your last Tinder date. The real kicker is when you successfully boot up the computer and it actually works. It's the most satisfying thing in the world, even though you might not understand why.

And then there’s the “Free Build” mode, where you can go wild and build your dream rig without the pressure of customer expectations. That’s when the true chaos starts. You’ll throw in the latest GPU, slap on 16 sticks of RAM, throw in a few RGB lights just to spite your bank account, and then try to figure out why your PC sounds like a jet engine taking off. But hey, at least it looks cool, right?

In conclusion, if you’ve ever thought about building a PC but feared the chaos of real-world mistakes (or the guilt of actually spending money), PC Building Simulator is the perfect way to prepare. It’s a hilarious, oddly therapeutic way to embrace your inner geek while quietly avoiding the inevitable disaster that is “replacing the thermal paste.
